title: Four rooms to live in
hookLine: kindness, compassion, gladness for others, equanimity: the "divine abodes" (DN 13)

cards: Where does your mind spend most of the day? Not your body, your mind. For a lot of people, it's a few familiar rooms.
The worry room. The irritation room, with the window that looks out on other people's mistakes. The comparison room, lined with other people's photos.
Nobody chooses to go in. A mind just finds itself there, again and again, out of habit. The Buddha described four other rooms, and taught a way to move into them.

teach.b: Today's word is brahmavihara. Brahma means divine, sublime, the highest. Vihara means a dwelling, a place you live; it's also the word for a monastery.
So brahmavihara is a divine abode, a sublime place to live. There are four. Metta, kindness: wishing others well.
Karuna, compassion: being moved by another's pain. Mudita, gladness at someone else's good fortune. And upekkha, equanimity: a balance that doesn't abandon anyone.
They're also called the four immeasurables, because they can grow without limit.

In the discourse on the three knowledges, two young brahmins come to the Buddha arguing about which teacher knows the way to union with Brahma, the god they worshiped. The Buddha doesn't mock their question.
He answers in their own language.

Someone who wants to live with Brahma, he says, should let a mind of kindness fill one direction, then the second, the third and the fourth, then above, below and all around, the whole world, boundless and free of hatred.
Then compassion the same way, then gladness, then equanimity.

teach.h: TWO YOUNG BRAHMINS ASK THE WAY.
teach.b: Buddhists read this in different ways.
Theravada teachers stress it as a meditation that calms the mind and supports insight.
Mahayana teachers see the four as the heart of the bodhisattva, who works for the good of all beings. You met metta in camp three.
The next two weeks walk through each room, along with what the old manuals call each room's enemies: a far enemy that's its opposite, and a near enemy that looks just like it.

how: Buddhists across traditions practice the four brahmaviharas, often by sending each quality out in all directions; Theravada teachers use them as meditation subjects, and Mahayana teachers speak of them as the heart of the bodhisattva's path.

o: a divine abode, a sublime place for the heart
a rule for how monks share their meals
a festival held at the start of the rains

games.q: match each room to its meaning.

s: vihara means a dwelling, and also a monastery
brahmavihara is a divine abode, a sublime place to live.
in the sutta, the Buddha mocks the young brahmins' question
he answers in their own language, with the four boundless states.
the four are also called the immeasurables
because they can grow without limit.

games.q: two young brahmins ask you the way to live with Brahma. what does the Buddha answer in the sutta?
o: tell them their question is foolish.
teach them to fill the whole world with kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity.
games.why: the Buddha answers in their own terms: let a mind of kindness, then compassion, gladness and equanimity fill every direction, boundless.

practice: Stand in each doorway for a few breaths.

Metta: let a warm wish for someone arise; karuna: remember someone who's struggling, and let your heart soften; mudita: think of someone who's doing well, and be glad; upekkha: let everything be as it is, for this moment.
Then rest in whichever room felt most like home.

wordCard.voice: Brahmavihara. A divine abode: kindness, compassion, gladness for others and equanimity, the four rooms to live in.

orig.note: Pali brahmavihāra: brahma (divine, sublime) and vihāra (dwelling): a divine abode.

carryVoice: Your line: boundless and free of hatred. Four rooms, each able to grow without limit. That's day two hundred thirty-two.
